Helly theorems for lattice of flats of a matroid

Amir Jafari Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Affiliation: New Uzbekistan University Affiliation: Tashkent, Uzbekistan Email: a.jafari@newuu.uz    Kiumars Kaveh Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Affiliation: University of Pittsburgh Affiliation: Pittsburgh, PA 15260, USA Email: kaveh@pitt.edu
Abstract

A basis of a matroid is adapted to a flat if it contains a basis of the flat. We prove that a family of flats in a rank rr matroid has a common adapted basis whenever every subfamily of at most r+1r+1 flats does. The ground set and the family may be infinite; only the rank must be finite. This result, in particular, contains Klyachko’s vector space Helly theorem for subspaces. As an application, we obtain a splitting criterion for tropical toric vector bundles on projective spaces. As a secondary application, we derive quadratic bounds for the Helly number for distributive generation in the lattice of flats.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 05B35; Secondary 06C10, 06D05, 52A35, 14T15.

Keywords. Matroid, adapted basis, Helly number, lattice of flats, distributive lattice, Bergman fan.

1 Introduction

Helly’s classical theorem asserts that a finite family of convex subsets of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} has nonempty intersection if every subfamily of at most n+1n+1 members has nonempty intersection [6]. In this paper, we prove an analogue of the Helly theorem for the lattice of flats of a matroid.

Let MM be a matroid of finite rank rr, with ground set EE. A basis BB of MM is said to be adapted to a flat FF if B∩FB\cap F is a basis of the restriction M|FM|F. A family of flats has a common adapted basis if there is a basis of MM that is adapted to every flat in the family. Our main result gives a sharp Helly theorem for the existence of such a basis.

Theorem 1.1 (Helly theorem for adapted bases).

Let MM be a matroid of finite rank rr, and let ℱ\mathcal{F} be any family of its flats. If every subfamily of at most r+1r+1 members has a common adapted basis, then ℱ\mathcal{F} has a common adapted basis. For every r≥2r\geq 2, the number r+1r+1 is optimal.

Neither the ground set nor the family of flats is required to be finite. For each flat FF, let ℬF\mathcal{B}_{F} denote the set of bases adapted to FF. Theorem 1.1 says that ⋂F∈ℱℬF\bigcap_{F\in\mathcal{F}}\mathcal{B}_{F} is nonempty whenever the intersection of every at most r+1r+1 of these sets is nonempty. Thus it is a Helly theorem in the literal intersection sense. We define the Helly number hcb​(r)h_{\mathrm{cb}}(r) to be the smallest number hh such that the following holds: for any family of flats, whenever any subfamily of at most hh flats has a common adapted basis then the whole family has a common adapted basis (cf. [7, Section 6]). Theorem 1.1 says that

hcb​(r)=r+1(r≥2).h_{\mathrm{cb}}(r)=r+1\qquad(r\geq 2).

To show that the r+1r+1 bound is sharp, consider the uniform matroid M=Ur,r+1M=U_{r,r+1} and take the family of r+1r+1 singleton flats in MM.

Our motivation comes from a remarkable theorem of Klyachko [12, Theorem 6.1.2], which gives the same r+1r+1 criterion for a finite collection of subspaces of an rr-dimensional vector space. Here a basis is adapted to a subspace when the subspace is spanned by a subset of the basis. Taking the matroid of all vectors in the ambient space recovers this statement from Theorem 1.1. We remark that Klyachko’s proof uses the modularity of dimension:

dimU+dimV=dim(U∩V)+dim(U+V).\dim U+\dim V=\dim(U\cap V)+\dim(U+V).

But for an arbitrary matroid, the rank function satisfies only the submodular inequality

rk⁡(F)+rk⁡(G)≥rk⁡(F∩G)+rk⁡(F∨G).\operatorname{rk}(F)+\operatorname{rk}(G)\geq\operatorname{rk}(F\cap G)+\operatorname{rk}(F\vee G).

We prove Theorem 1.1 by induction on rank and restriction to proper flats.

Theorem 1.1 has an application to tropical toric vector bundles. A toric vector bundle is a vector bundle on a toric variety together with a linear action of the torus. They have been classified in [12]. Motivated by Klyachko’s classification, Khan-Maclagan [11] and Kaveh-Manon [9] introduce a tropical version of toric vector bundles called tropical toric vector bundles.

The Bergman fan of a matroid is a union of subcomplexes, one for each matroid basis, called apartments (see [9]). Each apartment can be identified with the Coxeter complex of type A. In [9] a tropical toric vector bundle is described by a map from a fan to the Bergman fan of a matroid that is integral and piecewise linear in the sense that each cone maps to a an apartment in an integral linear way.

A toric vector bundle is said to be split if it is equivariantly isomorphic to a sum of toric line bundles. A toric vector bundle is split if the image of the corresponding piecewise linear map lands in one apartment in the extended Tits building (see [12, 10]). Motivated by this, a tropical toric vector bundle is said to be split when the image of its piecewise linear map lands in one apartment in the Bergman fan.

Corollary 1.2.

Every tropical toric vector bundle of rank r<nr<n on the fan of ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} is split.

A second theme of the paper concerns distributivity. For a finite collection of vector subspaces, the existence of a common adapted basis is equivalent to distributivity of the sublattice they generate under intersection and sum [12, §2.2.2]. This equivalence is a main step in Klyachko’s proof. For a matroid, a common adapted basis for a family of flats implies the distributivity of the lattice they generate: the flats spanned by subsets of a fixed basis form a Boolean sublattice of L⁡(M)L(M). The converse, however, is not true in general. For example, take the uniform matroid U3,4U_{3,4} on E={e1,e2,e3,e4}E=\{e_{1},e_{2},e_{3},e_{4}\}, the flats

F={e1,e2},G={e3,e4}F=\{e_{1},e_{2}\},\qquad G=\{e_{3},e_{4}\}

generate the four-element Boolean lattice {∅,F,G,E}\{\varnothing,F,G,E\}, but a basis adapted to both would have to contain all four elements. Proposition 4.4 identifies the precise additional condition: a finite family of flats has a common adapted basis if and only if the lattice it generates is distributive and rank is a valuation on that lattice.

This distinction motivates a separate Helly problem. For r≥2r\geq 2, define the distributive Helly number hdist​(r)h_{\mathrm{dist}}(r) to be the least positive integer hh such that, for every rank rr matroid and every family ℱ\mathcal{F} of its flats, the lattice generated by ℱ\mathcal{F} is distributive whenever every subfamily of at most hh members generates a distributive lattice. Our second main result establishes upper and lower bounds and determines the growth of this number up to an additive constant.

Theorem 1.3 (Bounds for distributive generation).

For every r≥2r\geq 2,

max⁡{r+1,⌊(r−1)24⌋}\displaystyle\max\left\{r+1,\left\lfloor\frac{(r-1)^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor\right\} ≤hdist​(r)\displaystyle\leq h_{\mathrm{dist}}(r)
≤max⁡{r+1, 2​r−3,⌊(r−1)24⌋+1}.\displaystyle\leq\max\left\{r+1,\;2r-3,\;\left\lfloor\frac{(r-1)^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor+1\right\}.
Remark 1.4.

When r>7r>7, the previous theorem says that

⌊(r−1)24⌋≤hdist​(r)≤⌊(r−1)24⌋+1.\left\lfloor\frac{(r-1)^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor\leq h_{\mathrm{dist}}(r)\leq\left\lfloor\frac{(r-1)^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor+1.

It can be proved that in fact hdist​(r)h_{\mathrm{dist}}(r) is equal to the above lower bound for r>6r>6, and is equal to r+1r+1 for r≤6r\leq 6. However, for the sake of brevity, we have omitted this proof.

Related work. Huang and Kaveh [7, §6] introduced Helly numbers of buildings, motivated by the splitting problem for toric principal bundles, and asked for sharp bounds. Tsvelikhovskiy [16] has recently studied Helly numbers for Tits buildings of connected reductive groups and the splitting of toric principal bundles. In another recent work of Tsvelikhovskiy et al [8], an analogue of Klyachko’s theorem is proved for modules over a DVR. Equivalently, this work computes the Helly number of the Bruhat-Tits building in type A. Theorem 1.1 can also be read in terms of common basis complexes. Rognes introduced the common basis complex of a vector space [15], Brück, Piterman, and Welker treat its analogue for matroids [2, §3.2], and Piterman, Shareshian, and Welker extend common basis complexes to spherical buildings [14]. These papers are mainly concerned with the topology of these complexes and of related posets of decompositions, and Theorem 1.1 is a statement of a different flavor. Take as vertices the flats of MM other than 0M0_{M} and EE, and as faces the finite sets of such flats with a common adapted basis. Theorem 1.1 says that every minimal nonface of this complex has at most r+1r+1 vertices.

Organization. Section 2 recalls the necessary matroid and lattice terminology. Section 3 proves the Helly theorem for adapted bases and its applications to flags and tropical toric vector bundles. Section 4 examines the relation between distributivity and existence of common adapted bases, and Section 5 proves the bounds for distributive generation.

2 Background on matroids and lattices

Throughout, we work with matroids of finite rank, but the ground sets are allowed to be infinite. We write EE for the ground set, rk\rk for the rank function, and cl\cl for closure. We use the usual independent set axioms. For standard matroid terminology, see [13].

Definition 2.1.

For r≥2r\geq 2, the (uniform) Helly number hcb​(r)h_{\mathrm{cb}}(r) is the least positive integer hh with the following property: for every rank rr matroid and every family of its flats, if each subfamily with at most hh members has a common adapted basis, then so does the entire family. (Here cb\mathrm{cb} stands for common basis.)

The Helly number is uniform over all matroids; the least number for a fixed matroid can be smaller. The main result of the paper (Theorem 3.1) shows that the uniform Helly number hcb​(r)h_{\mathrm{cb}}(r) is equal to r+1r+1.

The lattice of flats L⁡(M)L(M) has operations

F∧G=F∩G,F∨G=cl⁡(F∪G).F\wedge G=F\cap G,\qquad F\vee G=\cl(F\cup G).

Its bottom flat is 0M=cl⁡(∅)0_{M}=\cl(\varnothing), the set of loops; its top flat is EE. Empty joins mean 0M0_{M}. We retain loops throughout. The restriction to a flat FF is denoted by M|FM|F; its flats are exactly the flats of MM contained in FF. A basis of FF means a basis of M|FM|F, and is adapted to a flat W⊆FW\subseteq F when its intersection with WW is a basis of WW.

For a nonempty family ℱ\mathcal{F} of flats, ⟨ℱ⟩\langle\mathcal{F}\rangle denotes the sublattice generated by meets and joins. We put ⟨∅⟩=∅\langle\varnothing\rangle=\varnothing and regard the empty family as distributive. We do not automatically adjoin 0M,E0_{M},E. Note that adjoining a bottom or top flat does not affect distributivity. It can affect height, defined as the number of strict steps in a longest chain. Every sublattice of L⁡(M)L(M) has height at most rk⁡(M)\rk(M), since strict inclusion of flats increases rank. A finitely generated distributive lattice is finite: every term is a join of meets of subsets of its generators.

Definition 2.2.

Similarly, for r≥2r\geq 2, we define the (uniform) distributive Helly number hdist​(r)h_{\mathrm{dist}}(r) to be the least positive integer hh with the following property: for every rank rr matroid and every family of its flats, if each subfamily of at most hh members is distributive, then so is the entire family.

We note that if S,TS,T are subsets of a basis, then

cl⁡(S)∩cl⁡(T)=cl⁡(S∩T),cl⁡(S)∨cl⁡(T)=cl⁡(S∪T).\cl(S)\cap\cl(T)=\cl(S\cap T),\qquad\cl(S)\vee\cl(T)=\cl(S\cup T). (2.1)

A basis BB is adapted to FF precisely when F=cl⁡(B∩F)F=\cl(B\cap F). Also cl⁡(S)∩B=S\cl(S)\cap B=S, so the map S↦cl⁡(S)S\mapsto\cl(S) is injective on subsets of BB. Thus the flats to which BB is adapted form a Boolean sublattice of height rr with exactly 2r2^{r} elements. Every family with a common adapted basis generates a distributive sublattice. In particular, these facts apply to M|FM|F for every flat FF.

3 A Helly theorem for common adapted bases

In this section we prove the main result of the paper:

Theorem 3.1.

Let MM be a matroid of finite rank rr, and let ℱ\mathcal{F} be any family of its flats. If every subfamily of at most r+1r+1 members has a common adapted basis, then ℱ\mathcal{F} has a common adapted basis. Moreover, for r≥2r\geq 2 the number r+1r+1 cannot be replaced by rr, already for graphic matroids; thus hcb​(r)=r+1h_{\mathrm{cb}}(r)=r+1. In ranks zero and one, every family of flats has a common adapted basis.

The proof relies on the following two lemmas. We first treat finite families. Lemma 3.2 builds a finite set that is a basis on every intersection; Lemma 3.3 shows that this set can be extended to a common adapted basis.

Lemma 3.2.

Let ℱ={F1,…,Fm}\mathcal{F}=\{F_{1},\ldots,F_{m}\} be a nonempty family of flats, and put

ℐ={⋂i∈IFi:∅≠I⊆{1,…,m}}.\mathcal{I}=\left\{\bigcap_{i\in I}F_{i}:\varnothing\neq I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\right\}. (3.1)

Suppose that, for each ii, there is a basis BiB_{i} of M|FiM|F_{i} adapted to every W∈ℐW\in\mathcal{I} contained in FiF_{i}. Then there is a set Q⊆⋃iFiQ\subseteq\bigcup_{i}F_{i} such that Q∩WQ\cap W is a basis of WW for every W∈ℐW\in\mathcal{I}.

Proof.

For each W∈ℐW\in\mathcal{I}, let

TW=⋁U∈ℐU⊊WU.T_{W}=\bigvee_{\begin{subarray}{c}U\in\mathcal{I}\\ U\subsetneq W\end{subarray}}U.

Choose elements DW⊆W∖TWD_{W}\subseteq W\setminus T_{W} that extend a basis of TWT_{W} to a basis of WW. Thus

|DW|=rk⁡(W)−rk⁡(TW),cl⁡(TW∪DW)=W.|D_{W}|=\operatorname{rk}(W)-\operatorname{rk}(T_{W}),\qquad\operatorname{cl}(T_{W}\cup D_{W})=W.

Set Q=⋃W∈ℐDWQ=\bigcup_{W\in\mathcal{I}}D_{W}. From the construction, it follows that the DWD_{W} are pairwise disjoint: take W,U∈ℐW,U\in\mathcal{I} with W≠UW\neq U. Without loss of generality suppose U⊈WU\nsubseteq W, then

U∩W⊊U,U∩W⊆TU,U\cap W\subsetneq U,\qquad U\cap W\subseteq T_{U},

so DU∩W=∅D_{U}\cap W=\varnothing and hence DU∩DW=∅D_{U}\cap D_{W}=\varnothing. Consequently,

Q∩W=⨆U∈ℐU⊆WDU.Q\cap W=\bigsqcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}U\in\mathcal{I}\\ U\subseteq W\end{subarray}}D_{U}.

We now show that Q∩WQ\cap W is a basis of WW by induction on inclusion. For minimal WW, this follows directly from the choice of DWD_{W}. For the induction step, let U1,…,UsU_{1},\ldots,U_{s} be the maximal members of ℐ\mathcal{I} that are strictly contained in WW. Then

TW=U1∨⋯∨Us,Q∩W=Y⊔DW,whereY=⋃j=1s(Q∩Uj).T_{W}=U_{1}\vee\cdots\vee U_{s},\qquad Q\cap W=Y\sqcup D_{W},\quad\text{where}\quad Y=\bigcup_{j=1}^{s}(Q\cap U_{j}).

By induction, Q∩UjQ\cap U_{j} is a basis of UjU_{j}, so YY already spans TWT_{W}. It remains to show |Y|=rk⁡(TW)|Y|=\operatorname{rk}(T_{W}). Choose ii such that W⊆FiW\subseteq F_{i}. This is where we use the assumption of existence of the basis BiB_{i}. For every nonempty J⊆{1,…,s}J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,s\}, put

VJ=⋂j∈JUj.V_{J}=\bigcap_{j\in J}U_{j}.

This intersection belongs to ℐ\mathcal{I}, is properly contained in WW, and lies in FiF_{i}. Therefore by induction, Q∩VJQ\cap V_{J} is a basis of VJV_{J}. Also by the assumption on BiB_{i}, Bi∩VJB_{i}\cap V_{J} is a basis of VJV_{J}. Hence

|Q∩VJ|=|Bi∩VJ|=rk⁡(VJ).|Q\cap V_{J}|=|B_{i}\cap V_{J}|=\operatorname{rk}(V_{J}).

Now we apply the inclusion–exclusion principle to the union of finite sets Q∩UjQ\cap U_{j}:

|Y|\displaystyle|Y| =∑∅≠J⊆[s](−1)|J|+1​|Q∩VJ|\displaystyle=\sum_{\varnothing\neq J\subseteq[s]}(-1)^{|J|+1}|Q\cap V_{J}|
=∑∅≠J⊆[s](−1)|J|+1​rk⁡(VJ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\varnothing\neq J\subseteq[s]}(-1)^{|J|+1}\operatorname{rk}(V_{J})
=∑∅≠J⊆[s](−1)|J|+1​|Bi∩VJ|\displaystyle=\sum_{\varnothing\neq J\subseteq[s]}(-1)^{|J|+1}|B_{i}\cap V_{J}|
=|⋃j=1s(Bi∩Uj)|.\displaystyle=\left|\bigcup_{j=1}^{s}(B_{i}\cap U_{j})\right|.

Write A=⋃j(Bi∩Uj)A=\bigcup_{j}(B_{i}\cap U_{j}). Because A⊆BiA\subseteq B_{i}, it is independent. Because Bi∩UjB_{i}\cap U_{j} spans UjU_{j} for every jj, AA spans TWT_{W}. Thus

|Y|=|A|=rk⁡(TW),|Y|=|A|=\operatorname{rk}(T_{W}),

as desired. Finally, Y∪DW=Q∩WY\cup D_{W}=Q\cap W spans WW, and

|Q∩W|=rk⁡(TW)+(rk⁡(W)−rk⁡(TW))=rk⁡(W).|Q\cap W|=\operatorname{rk}(T_{W})+\bigl(\operatorname{rk}(W)-\operatorname{rk}(T_{W})\bigr)=\operatorname{rk}(W).

It is therefore a basis of WW.

The important point is that matroid rank does not generally satisfy inclusion–exclusion. The basis BiB_{i} allows the relevant ranks to be interpreted as cardinalities of subsets of one independent set, where inclusion–exclusion does apply. ∎

Lemma 3.3.

Let MM be a rank rr matroid, and let ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℐ\mathcal{I} be as in (3.1). Suppose Q⊆⋃iFiQ\subseteq\bigcup_{i}F_{i} and Q∩WQ\cap W is a basis of WW for every W∈ℐW\in\mathcal{I}. If QQ is dependent then there is J⊆{1,…,m}J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}, with |J|≤r+1|J|\leq r+1, such that

∑∅≠K⊆J(−1)|K|+1​rk⁡(⋂k∈KFk)>rk⁡(⋃j∈JFj).\sum_{\varnothing\neq K\subseteq J}(-1)^{|K|+1}\rk\!\left(\bigcap_{k\in K}F_{k}\right)>\rk\!\left(\bigcup_{j\in J}F_{j}\right). (3.2)

In particular, the flats FjF_{j}, j∈Jj\in J, have no common adapted basis.

Proof.

Choose a circuit C⊆QC\subseteq Q. Pick FjF_{j}, j∈Jj\in J such that C⊂⋃j∈JFjC\subset\bigcup_{j\in J}F_{j} and |J|≤|C|≤r+1|J|\leq|C|\leq r+1. Put U=⋃j∈JFjU=\bigcup_{j\in J}F_{j}. Note that UU may not be a flat itself. The finite set Q∩UQ\cap U spans UU and contains CC, so |Q∩U|>rk⁡(U):=rk⁡(cl⁡(U))|Q\cap U|>\rk(U):=\rk(\cl(U)). The inclusion-exclusion applied to the sets Q∩FjQ\cap F_{j}, j∈Jj\in J, shows that |Q∩U||Q\cap U| coincides with the left-hand side of (3.2) which proves the first claim. To prove the second claim, suppose a basis BB is adapted to the flats FjF_{j}, j∈Jj\in J. Then, for any subset K⊂JK\subset J, BB is adapted to ⋂k∈KFk\bigcap_{k\in K}F_{k}. Using inclusion-exclusion for the subsets B∩FjB\cap F_{j}, j∈Jj\in J, we get |B∩U|=rk⁡(U)|B\cap U|=\rk(U) which contradicts (3.2). ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

First suppose the family is finite. We prove the claim by induction on the rank rr. The cases r=0,1r=0,1 are immediate. Discard the bottom flat 0M0_{M} and the top flat EE, to which every basis is adapted. Write the remaining family as {F1,…,Fm}\{F_{1},\ldots,F_{m}\}, and let ℐ\mathcal{I} be as in (3.1).

Fix ii and put k=rk⁡(Fi)k=\rk(F_{i}), so 1≤k<r1\leq k<r. In the restriction M|FiM|F_{i}, consider the flats Fi∩FjF_{i}\cap F_{j}. Since k+2≤r+1k+2\leq r+1, any k+1k+1 of the FjF_{j} together with FiF_{i} have a common adapted basis. This implies that any k+1k+1 of the Fi∩FjF_{i}\cap F_{j} have a common adapted basis. The induction hypothesis then gives a basis BiB_{i} of FiF_{i} adapted to all the Fi∩FjF_{i}\cap F_{j}, and hence to all their intersections. In fact, if W=⋂j∈JFj⊆FiW=\bigcap_{j\in J}F_{j}\subseteq F_{i}, then W=⋂j∈J(Fi∩Fj)W=\bigcap_{j\in J}(F_{i}\cap F_{j}), so BiB_{i} is adapted to every member of ℐ\mathcal{I} contained in FiF_{i}.

Now by Lemma 3.2, we have a set Q⊆⋃iFiQ\subseteq\bigcup_{i}F_{i} meeting each member of ℐ\mathcal{I} in a basis. Lemma 3.3 and the hypothesis imply that QQ is independent. Extend the set QQ to a basis BB of MM. Since Q∩FiQ\cap F_{i} already spans FiF_{i}, the basis BB adds no element of FiF_{i}. Thus B∩Fi=Q∩FiB\cap F_{i}=Q\cap F_{i}, so BB is adapted to every flat FiF_{i}.

Now suppose ℱ\mathcal{F} is possibly infinite and satisfies the local hypothesis, that is, any r+1r+1 subfamily has an adapted basis. By what we just proved, every finite subfamily has a common adapted basis. If ℱ\mathcal{F} contained 2r+12^{r}+1 distinct flats, these could not all admit one adapted basis, since a basis, which has rr elements, is adapted to exactly 2r2^{r} flats. Hence ℱ\mathcal{F} itself has at most 2r2^{r} distinct members, and the finite-family result applies.

To prove that the r+1r+1 bound is sharp, take the uniform matroid Ur,r+1U_{r,r+1}, whose independent sets are the subsets of size at most rr. Its r+1r+1 singleton flats have no common adapted basis, while any rr do. Note that Ur,r+1U_{r,r+1} is the graphic matroid of a cycle with r+1r+1 edges. ∎

For any field KK, take the rank rr matroid consisting of all vectors in KrK^{r}, including the zero vector as a loop. Its flats are exactly the linear subspaces. Theorem 3.1 therefore recovers Klyachko’s theorem over every field.

A flag is a chain of flats; a basis is adapted to a collection of flags if it is adapted to every flat occurring in them. The following is an immediate corollary of Theorem 3.1.

Corollary 3.4.

A collection of flags in a matroid of rank rr has a common adapted basis if every subcollection of at most r+1r+1 flags does.

For a finite loopless matroid MM on EE, the support of its Bergman fan is

Berg(M)={w∈ℝE:mine∈Dwe is attained at least twice for every circuit D}.\operatorname{Berg}(M)=\{w\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:\min_{e\in D}w_{e}\text{ is attained at least twice for every circuit }D\}.

Its fine subdivision has cones indexed by flags of flats [1, 5]. For a basis BB, its apartment is

AB={w∈Berg⁡(M):w⁡(B)≥w⁡(B′)​ for every basis ​B′},w⁡(S)=∑e∈Swe.A_{B}=\{w\in\operatorname{Berg}(M):w(B)\geq w(B^{\prime})\text{ for every basis }B^{\prime}\},\qquad w(S)=\sum_{e\in S}w_{e}.

A point ww lies in ABA_{B} exactly when BB is adapted to every flat in its flag of sets {e:we≥t}\{e:w_{e}\geq t\} [9, Definition 3.6 and Proposition 3.7]. Thus Corollary 3.4 gives the following.

Corollary 3.5.

A collection of points in the Bergman fan of a finite loopless rank rr matroid lies in one apartment if every subcollection of at most r+1r+1 points does. For r≥2r\geq 2, this is the optimal uniform bound over rank rr matroids.

Proof.

Apply Corollary 3.4 to the flags {e:we≥t}\{e:w_{e}\geq t\}, for ww in the given collection of points in the Bergman fan. For sharpness, in Ur,r+1U_{r,r+1} take the singleton indicator vectors wi=𝟏{i}w_{i}=\mathbf{1}_{\{i\}}. They belong to the Bergman fan, and wi∈ABw_{i}\in A_{B} exactly when i∈Bi\in B. Any rr points therefore lie in an apartment, whereas all r+1r+1 do not. ∎

We next deduce a splitting result for tropical toric vector bundles. This is a tropical extension of Klyachko’s result on splitting of toric vector bundles over projective space [12]. A tropical toric vector bundle is described by a map Φ:|Σ|→Berg⁡(M)\Phi:|\Sigma|\to\operatorname{Berg}(M) that, on each cone of Σ\Sigma, is integral and linear in the coordinates of some apartment [9, Definition 4.1]. It is called split when its entire image lies in one apartment [9, Definition 9.1].

Corollary 3.6.

A tropical toric vector bundle of rank r<nr<n on the fan of ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} is split.

Proof.

Any at most r+1≤nr+1\leq n rays belong to one cone. So their images lie in one apartment. Corollary 3.5 then implies that all the images of rays lie in one apartment ABA_{B}, for some basis BB. It remains to show that the whole image of Φ\Phi lands in ABA_{B}. But this is a consequence of the piecewise linearity of Φ\Phi. ∎

Remark 3.7.

The condition r<nr<n is optimal for n≥2n\geq 2. Let the underlying matroid be Un,n+1U_{n,n+1} on the ground set {0,…,n}\{0,\ldots,n\} and let v0,…,vnv_{0},\ldots,v_{n} be the rays of the fan of ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}. On the maximal cone omitting vjv_{j}, define, for x=∑i≠jλi​vix=\sum_{i\neq j}\lambda_{i}v_{i} with λi≥0\lambda_{i}\geq 0,

Φi​(x)=λi​(i≠j),Φj​(x)=mini≠j⁡λi.\Phi_{i}(x)=\lambda_{i}\ (i\neq j),\qquad\Phi_{j}(x)=\min_{i\neq j}\lambda_{i}.

These formulas agree on overlaps and are integral and linear in the apartment coordinates of A{0,…,n}∖{j}A_{\{0,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{j\}}. They define a rank nn bundle whose images of rays are standard basis vectors. But the standard basis vectors do not lie in one apartment, which proves that it is not split.

4 Distributivity and common adapted bases

A common adapted basis implies distributivity of the generated lattice (Section 2). The converse requires one additional condition: rank must be a valuation. We prove this criterion in Proposition 4.4 and deduce the full-height case needed in Section 5.

4.1 Adapted bases and valuations

A real-valued function vv on a lattice LL is a valuation if

v⁡(X)+v⁡(Y)=v⁡(X∧Y)+v⁡(X∨Y)for all ​X,Y∈L.v(X)+v(Y)=v(X\wedge Y)+v(X\vee Y)\qquad\text{for all }X,Y\in L. (4.1)

This identity is automatic for comparable pairs. Cardinality is a valuation on a lattice of finite sets under union and intersection, and dimension is a valuation on the lattice of vector subspaces. Matroid rank satisfies only

rk⁡(X)+rk⁡(Y)≥rk⁡(X∧Y)+rk⁡(X∨Y),\rk(X)+\rk(Y)\geq\rk(X\wedge Y)+\rk(X\vee Y),

both for sets, with join given by union, and for flats, with join given by closure of the union. Thus rank is a valuation precisely when equality holds for every pair in the lattice.

4.2 Birkhoff’s theorem

For a finite poset Π\Pi, let J⁡(Π)J(\Pi) be its lattice of order ideals: subsets I⊆ΠI\subseteq\Pi such that p∈Ip\in I and q≤pq\leq p imply q∈Iq\in I. Its meet and join are intersection and union. For p∈Πp\in\Pi, write

Ip={q∈Π:q≤p},Ip−=Ip∖{p}.I_{p}=\{q\in\Pi:q\leq p\},\qquad I_{p}^{-}=I_{p}\setminus\{p\}.

An element of a finite lattice is join-irreducible if it is not the least element and is not the join of two strictly smaller elements. In J⁡(Π)J(\Pi) these are exactly the principal ideals IpI_{p}.

Theorem 4.1 (Birkhoff).

Let DD be a finite distributive lattice, and let Π\Pi be the set of join-irreducible elements of DD, ordered as in DD. Then

D⟶J⁡(Π),x⟼{p∈Π:p≤x},D\longrightarrow J(\Pi),\qquad x\longmapsto\{p\in\Pi:p\leq x\},

is an isomorphism of lattices. Its inverse sends an ideal II to the join ⋁I\bigvee I, the join of the empty ideal being the least element of DD.

See [3, Chapter 5]. Every maximal chain in J⁡(Π)J(\Pi) has the form

∅=K0⊊K1⊊⋯⊊Kn=Π,Kk=Kk−1∪{pk},\varnothing=K_{0}\subsetneq K_{1}\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq K_{n}=\Pi,\qquad K_{k}=K_{k-1}\cup\{p_{k}\}, (4.2)

where p1,…,pnp_{1},\ldots,p_{n} lists the elements of Π\Pi in an order compatible with the partial order. Indeed, between two ideals one can add a minimal element of their difference. Hence DD has height |Π||\Pi|, and every ideal II occurs at position |I||I| on some maximal chain.

Example 4.2.

Let Π={a,b,c}\Pi=\{a,b,c\} with a<ca<c and b<cb<c, and a,ba,b incomparable. Then

J⁡(Π)={∅,{a},{b},{a,b},Π}.J(\Pi)=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b\},\Pi\}.

Its join-irreducibles are {a},{b},Π\{a\},\{b\},\Pi, and its two maximal chains correspond to the orders a,b,ca,b,c and b,a,cb,a,c. Both have length 33.

Lemma 4.3.

Let vv be a valuation on J⁡(Π)J(\Pi), and put

δp​(v)=v⁡(Ip)−v⁡(Ip−)(p∈Π).\delta_{p}(v)=v(I_{p})-v(I_{p}^{-})\qquad(p\in\Pi).
  1. (a)

    If II and I∪{p}I\cup\{p\} are ideals and p∉Ip\notin I, then v⁡(I∪{p})=v⁡(I)+δp​(v)v(I\cup\{p\})=v(I)+\delta_{p}(v).

  2. (b)

    For every ideal II,

    v⁡(I)=v⁡(∅)+∑p∈Iδp​(v).v(I)=v(\varnothing)+\sum_{p\in I}\delta_{p}(v).
  3. (c)

    Two valuations on J⁡(Π)J(\Pi) that agree on one maximal chain agree everywhere.

Conversely, for any real numbers cc and cpc_{p} (p∈Π)(p\in\Pi), the function I↦c+∑p∈IcpI\mapsto c+\sum_{p\in I}c_{p} is a valuation on J⁡(Π)J(\Pi).

Proof.

In (a), Ip−⊆II_{p}^{-}\subseteq I and p∉Ip\notin I, so

I∩Ip=Ip−,I∪Ip=I∪{p}.I\cap I_{p}=I_{p}^{-},\qquad I\cup I_{p}=I\cup\{p\}.

Applying (4.1) to I,IpI,I_{p} gives (a). Adding the elements of II in an order compatible with the partial order gives (b). Along a maximal chain (4.2), the successive differences are the increments δpk​(v)\delta_{p_{k}}(v), each occurring once. Thus the chain determines v⁡(∅)v(\varnothing) and all increments, which proves (c). The converse follows from inclusion–exclusion. ∎

4.3 The criterion

Proposition 4.4.

Let MM be a finite-rank matroid and ℱ\mathcal{F} a finite nonempty family of its flats. Let D=⟨ℱ⟩D=\langle\mathcal{F}\rangle, and let ℛ\mathcal{R} be the lattice of subsets generated by ℱ\mathcal{F} under set-theoretic union and intersection. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    ℱ\mathcal{F} has a common adapted basis.

  2. (ii)

    DD is distributive and rank is a valuation on DD.

  3. (iii)

    Rank is a valuation on ℛ\mathcal{R}.

The lattice ℛ\mathcal{R} is automatically distributive, but its members need not be flats: its join is union, rather than closure of the union.

Proof.

(i)⇒\Rightarrow(ii). Let BB be a common adapted basis. By (2.1), the flats cl⁡(S)\cl(S), S⊆BS\subseteq B, form a Boolean sublattice containing ℱ\mathcal{F}, and hence DD. Under the isomorphism S↦cl⁡(S)S\mapsto\cl(S), rank is cardinality. Thus DD is distributive and rank is a valuation on DD.

(i)⇒\Rightarrow(iii). For the same basis BB, let

𝒮={A⊆E:A⊆cl⁡(B∩A)}.\mathcal{S}=\{A\subseteq E:A\subseteq\cl(B\cap A)\}.

This family contains ℱ\mathcal{F} and is closed under unions. It is also closed under intersections, since for A,A′∈𝒮A,A^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S},

A∩A′⊆cl⁡(B∩A)∩cl⁡(B∩A′)=cl⁡(B∩A∩A′)A\cap A^{\prime}\subseteq\cl(B\cap A)\cap\cl(B\cap A^{\prime})=\cl(B\cap A\cap A^{\prime})

by (2.1). Hence ℛ⊆𝒮\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{S}, so B∩AB\cap A is a basis of AA for every A∈ℛA\in\mathcal{R}. Therefore rk⁡(A)=|B∩A|\rk(A)=|B\cap A| on ℛ\mathcal{R}, a valuation by inclusion–exclusion.

(ii)⇒\Rightarrow(i). Since DD is finitely generated and distributive, it is finite. Write D=J⁡(Π)D=J(\Pi) by Theorem 4.1, and denote the flat corresponding to II by FIF_{I}. Thus

FI∪I′=FI∨FI′,FI∩I′=FI∩FI′.F_{I\cup I^{\prime}}=F_{I}\vee F_{I^{\prime}},\qquad F_{I\cap I^{\prime}}=F_{I}\cap F_{I^{\prime}}.

The least flat F∅F_{\varnothing} of DD need not equal 0M0_{M}. Choose a basis B∅B_{\varnothing} of it. For each p∈Πp\in\Pi, extend a basis of FIp−F_{I_{p}^{-}} to a basis of FIpF_{I_{p}}, and let ApA_{p} be the set of added elements. Then

|Ap|=δp:=rk⁡(FIp)−rk⁡(FIp−),|A_{p}|=\delta_{p}:=\rk(F_{I_{p}})-\rk(F_{I_{p}^{-}}),

and

cl⁡(FIp−∪Ap)=FIp.\cl(F_{I_{p}^{-}}\cup A_{p})=F_{I_{p}}. (4.3)

For each ideal II, put

BI=B∅∪⋃p∈IAp.B_{I}=B_{\varnothing}\cup\bigcup_{p\in I}A_{p}.

We show by induction on |I||I| that BIB_{I} is a basis of FIF_{I}. The case I=∅I=\varnothing holds by construction. Otherwise choose a maximal element pp of II and put I′=I∖{p}I^{\prime}=I\setminus\{p\}. By induction, BI′B_{I^{\prime}} spans FI′F_{I^{\prime}}, which contains FIp−F_{I_{p}^{-}}. Thus (4.3) shows that BI=BI′∪ApB_{I}=B_{I^{\prime}}\cup A_{p} spans

FI′∨FIp=FI.F_{I^{\prime}}\vee F_{I_{p}}=F_{I}.

Also BI⊆FIB_{I}\subseteq F_{I}, and Lemma 4.3(a) gives

|BI|≤|BI′|+|Ap|=rk⁡(FI′)+δp=rk⁡(FI).|B_{I}|\leq|B_{I^{\prime}}|+|A_{p}|=\rk(F_{I^{\prime}})+\delta_{p}=\rk(F_{I}).

Hence BIB_{I} is a basis of FIF_{I}. Extend BΠB_{\Pi} to a basis BB of MM. For every II, the independent set B∩FIB\cap F_{I} contains the basis BIB_{I} of FIF_{I}, so B∩FI=BIB\cap F_{I}=B_{I}. Thus BB is adapted to all members of DD.

(iii)⇒\Rightarrow(i). The lattice ℛ\mathcal{R} is finite, since every member is a union of intersections of the finitely many generators. Adjoin ∅,E\varnothing,E to obtain ℛ+\mathcal{R}^{+}. Rank remains a valuation, since the added sets are comparable with every member. Choose a maximal chain

∅=C0⊊C1⊊⋯⊊Cn=E.\varnothing=C_{0}\subsetneq C_{1}\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq C_{n}=E.

Starting with B0=∅B_{0}=\varnothing, successively extend a basis Bk−1B_{k-1} of Ck−1C_{k-1} to a basis BkB_{k} of CkC_{k}, and put B=BnB=B_{n}. Then B∩Ck=BkB\cap C_{k}=B_{k}, so

|B∩Ck|=rk⁡(Ck)(0≤k≤n).|B\cap C_{k}|=\rk(C_{k})\qquad(0\leq k\leq n).

The valuations A↦rk⁡(A)A\mapsto\rk(A) and A↦|B∩A|A\mapsto|B\cap A| on the finite distributive lattice ℛ+\mathcal{R}^{+} agree on this chain, and hence everywhere by Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 4.3(c). In particular BB is adapted to every F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}. ∎

Example 4.5.

Let M=U3,4M=U_{3,4} on E={e1,e2,e3,e4}E=\{e_{1},e_{2},e_{3},e_{4}\}, and take F={e1,e2}F=\{e_{1},e_{2}\} and G={e2,e3}G=\{e_{2},e_{3}\}. Then

⟨F,G⟩={{e2},F,G,E}\langle F,G\rangle=\bigl\{\{e_{2}\},F,G,E\bigr\}

is Boolean, and rank is a valuation since 2+2=1+32+2=1+3. In the preceding construction the two join-irreducibles have increments one. Taking B∅={e2}B_{\varnothing}=\{e_{2}\}, AF={e1}A_{F}=\{e_{1}\} and AG={e3}A_{G}=\{e_{3}\} gives the common adapted basis {e1,e2,e3}\{e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}\}.

Corollary 4.6.

A finite distributive sublattice of height rr in the lattice of flats of a rank rr matroid has a common adapted basis.

Proof.

Write the sublattice as J⁡(Π)J(\Pi), with corresponding flats FIF_{I}. Its height is |Π|=r|\Pi|=r. Along any maximal chain there are rr strict rank increases, whose sum is at most rr. Each increase is therefore one, and the least flat has rank zero. Since every ideal II occurs at position |I||I| on some maximal chain, rk⁡(FI)=|I|\rk(F_{I})=|I| for all II. Thus rank is a valuation, and Proposition 4.4 applies. ∎

4.4 The rank condition cannot be omitted

Dimension is a valuation on the lattice of vector subspaces, so in that setting distributivity alone gives a common adapted basis [12, §2.2.2]. For matroid flats the additional rank condition is essential.

Example 4.7.

In U3,4U_{3,4}, take F={e1,e2}F=\{e_{1},e_{2}\} and G={e3,e4}G=\{e_{3},e_{4}\}. These flats generate the Boolean lattice {∅,F,G,E}\{\varnothing,F,G,E\}, but

rk⁡(F)+rk⁡(G)=4>3=rk⁡(F∧G)+rk⁡(F∨G).\rk(F)+\rk(G)=4>3=\rk(F\wedge G)+\rk(F\vee G).

A common adapted basis would contain all four elements, which is impossible in rank three.

Rank three is minimal for this phenomenon. In rank at most two, any incomparable flats have rank one, their meet has rank zero and their join has rank two. Thus rank is a valuation on the whole lattice of flats, and Proposition 4.4 applies to every finite family generating a distributive lattice.

The example is representable over every field KK: for a basis v1,v2,v3v_{1},v_{2},v_{3} of K3K^{3}, use the vectors

v1,v2,v3,v1+v2+v3.v_{1},\quad v_{2},\quad v_{3},\quad v_{1}+v_{2}+v_{3}.

Any three are independent. The spans of FF and GG meet in the line ⟨v1+v2⟩\langle v_{1}+v_{2}\rangle, although F∩G=∅F\cap G=\varnothing. Thus the span map preserves joins but not meets. The ambient basis v1,v1+v2,v3v_{1},v_{1}+v_{2},v_{3} is adapted to both planes, but it uses a vector outside the representing set.

5 Helly numbers for distributive generation

In this section we prove quadratic bounds for hdist​(r)h_{\mathrm{dist}}(r). Recall that a family ℱ\mathcal{F} is distributive if ⟨ℱ⟩\langle\mathcal{F}\rangle satisfies

x∧(y∨z)=(x∧y)∨(x∧z)x\wedge(y\vee z)=(x\wedge y)\vee(x\wedge z) (5.1)

for all x,y,zx,y,z, or equivalently the dual identity. The upper bound uses Theorem 3.1 and a bound on irredundant generators of finite distributive lattices. The lower bound comes from graphic matroids.

Theorem 5.1.

For every r≥2r\geq 2,

hdist​(r)≥{r+1,2≤r≤6,⌊(r−1)2/4⌋,r≥7,hdist​(r)≤{r+1,2≤r≤4,2​r−3,5≤r≤7,⌊(r−1)2/4⌋+1,r≥8.h_{\mathrm{dist}}(r)\geq\begin{cases}r+1,&2\leq r\leq 6,\\ \left\lfloor(r-1)^{2}/4\right\rfloor,&r\geq 7,\end{cases}\qquad h_{\mathrm{dist}}(r)\leq\begin{cases}r+1,&2\leq r\leq 4,\\ 2r-3,&5\leq r\leq 7,\\ \left\lfloor(r-1)^{2}/4\right\rfloor+1,&r\geq 8.\end{cases}

The same bounds hold when the distributive Helly number is restricted to graphic matroids, or to matroids representable over any prescribed field.

Thus hdist​(r)=(r−1)2/4+O⁡(1)h_{\mathrm{dist}}(r)=(r-1)^{2}/4+O(1), whereas hcb​(r)=r+1h_{\mathrm{cb}}(r)=r+1. The distributive bounds coincide for 2≤r≤42\leq r\leq 4 and differ by one for r≥8r\geq 8. Table 1 gives the values in small ranks.

5.1 Minimal failures

A minimal failure of distributive generation is a finite family that is not distributive but whose proper subfamilies are. A family 𝒳\mathcal{X} in a lattice is irredundant if no member belongs to the sublattice generated by the others. As before, we use only binary meets and joins, without adjoining endpoints.

Lemma 5.2.
  1. (a)

    Every family of flats that is not distributive contains a minimal failure.

  2. (b)

    A minimal failure and all its subfamilies are irredundant.

  3. (c)

    If a rank rr matroid has a minimal failure with mm members, then hdist​(r)≥mh_{\mathrm{dist}}(r)\geq m. If every minimal failure in every rank rr matroid has at most NN members, then hdist​(r)≤Nh_{\mathrm{dist}}(r)\leq N.

Proof.

(a) A violation of (5.1) involves three lattice terms, hence only finitely many generators. Choose a minimal subfamily among these generators that is not distributive.

(b) If a member were generated by the others, deleting it would leave the same nondistributive lattice, contrary to minimality. Every subfamily of an irredundant family is irredundant.

(c) A minimal failure with mm members disproves the Helly property for every h<mh<m. Conversely, by (a), every failure contains a minimal one; if its size is at most NN, it violates the local hypothesis for h=Nh=N. ∎

Example 5.3.

The r+1r+1 singleton flats of Ur,r+1U_{r,r+1}, r≥2r\geq 2, form a minimal failure. Every proper subfamily has a common adapted basis and is therefore distributive. For the whole family, take distinct singletons F,GF,G and let ZZ be the join of the remaining r−1r-1. Then Z∨G=EZ\vee G=E, while F∧Z=F∧G=∅F\wedge Z=F\wedge G=\varnothing, so

F∧(Z∨G)=F≠∅=(F∧Z)∨(F∧G).F\wedge(Z\vee G)=F\neq\varnothing=(F\wedge Z)\vee(F\wedge G).

Since Ur,r+1U_{r,r+1} is the cycle matroid of a cycle of length r+1r+1, this gives hdist​(r)≥r+1h_{\mathrm{dist}}(r)\geq r+1 already for graphic matroids.

5.2 Irredundant generators

Let g⁡(n)g(n) be the supremum of the sizes of irredundant families in finite distributive lattices of height at most nn, and put

f⁡(n)=max⁡{2​n−2,⌊n2/4⌋}(n≥1).f(n)=\max\{2n-2,\lfloor n^{2}/4\rfloor\}\qquad(n\geq 1).

We will prove that g⁡(n)=f⁡(n)g(n)=f(n) for n≥3n\geq 3. By Birkhoff’s theorem, we may first consider lattices of sets. For α,β\alpha,\beta in a finite set Ω\Omega, the subsets satisfying

α∈S⟹β∈S\alpha\in S\ \Longrightarrow\ \beta\in S (5.2)

form a sublattice of 2Ω2^{\Omega}. Thus a set that violates an implication satisfied by all the others cannot be generated by them.

A directed graph is reduced if it has no loops or parallel arcs, and no arc whose head can be reached from its tail by a directed path avoiding that arc.

Lemma 5.4.

Let S1,…,SmS_{1},\ldots,S_{m} be an irredundant family of nonempty proper subsets of a finite set Ω\Omega. For each ii there are αi∈Si\alpha_{i}\in S_{i} and βi∉Si\beta_{i}\notin S_{i} such that every SjS_{j} with j≠ij\neq i satisfies αi∈Sj⇒βi∈Sj\alpha_{i}\in S_{j}\Rightarrow\beta_{i}\in S_{j}. The arcs αi→βi\alpha_{i}\to\beta_{i} are distinct and form a reduced directed graph on Ω\Omega.

Proof.

Suppose no such pair exists for SiS_{i}. For every α∈Si\alpha\in S_{i} and β∉Si\beta\notin S_{i}, some SjS_{j}, j≠ij\neq i, contains α\alpha but not β\beta. For each α∈Si\alpha\in S_{i}, let NαN_{\alpha} be the intersection of the sets SjS_{j}, j≠ij\neq i, containing α\alpha. This collection of sets is nonempty since SiS_{i} is proper, and α∈Nα⊆Si\alpha\in N_{\alpha}\subseteq S_{i}. Hence

Si=⋃α∈SiNα,S_{i}=\bigcup_{\alpha\in S_{i}}N_{\alpha},

contrary to irredundance.

Choose such a witness pair (αi,βi)(\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}) for each ii. Its arc is not a loop. Two arcs cannot agree, since the corresponding sets would both violate the same implication. Also, SiS_{i} satisfies every implication except its own. A directed path from αi\alpha_{i} to βi\beta_{i} using other arcs would therefore imply βi∈Si\beta_{i}\in S_{i}, a contradiction. ∎

Example 5.5.

On Ω={1,2,3}\Omega=\{1,2,3\} the sets

{1},{1,2},{3},{2,3}\{1\},\qquad\{1,2\},\qquad\{3\},\qquad\{2,3\}

have witness pairs (1,2)(1,2), (2,3)(2,3), (3,2)(3,2) and (2,1)(2,1), respectively. Thus they are irredundant. Their witness graph is the path 1,2,31,2,3 with both orientations of each edge; it has 2⋅3−22\cdot 3-2 arcs.

Lemma 5.6.

A reduced directed graph on t≥1t\geq 1 vertices has at most f⁡(t)f(t) arcs.

Proof.

Let the strongly connected components have sizes s1,…,sks_{1},\ldots,s_{k}, with ∑csc=t\sum_{c}s_{c}=t. In a component of size ss, choose a root and spanning trees directed towards and away from it. Their union is strongly connected and has at most 2​s−22s-2 arcs. Every arc of the component must belong to this union, since otherwise it would have an alternative directed path. Thus there are at most 2​s−22s-2 internal arcs.

There is at most one arc from one component to another: a second such arc, together with paths inside the two components, would make the first redundant. The condensation is acyclic. If its underlying graph contained a triangle, its acyclic orientation would give an arc and an alternative two-step route, again contradicting reducedness. Mantel’s theorem [4, Chapter 7] therefore bounds the number of arcs between components by ⌊k2/4⌋\lfloor k^{2}/4\rfloor. The total is at most

∑c=1k(2​sc−2)+⌊k24⌋=⌊2​(t−k)+k24⌋.\sum_{c=1}^{k}(2s_{c}-2)+\left\lfloor\frac{k^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor 2(t-k)+\frac{k^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor.

The expression inside the floor is convex in kk. Its endpoint values on 1≤k≤t1\leq k\leq t are 2​t−2+1/42t-2+1/4 and t2/4t^{2}/4, which give the bound f⁡(t)f(t). ∎

Proposition 5.7.

We have g⁡(1)=2g(1)=2, g⁡(2)=3g(2)=3, and, for n≥3n\geq 3,

g⁡(n)≤f⁡(n)=max⁡{2​n−2,⌊n24⌋}.g(n)\leq f(n)=\max\left\{2n-2,\left\lfloor\frac{n^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor\right\}.
Proof.

A lattice of height at most one has at most two elements, and the two-element chain is irredundant. A distributive lattice of height two is either the three-element chain or the four-element Boolean lattice: any three elements strictly between its endpoints would form an M3M_{3}. The chain is irredundant, whereas the four elements of the Boolean lattice are not. Hence g⁡(1)=2g(1)=2 and g⁡(2)=3g(2)=3.

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a nonempty irredundant family, and replace its ambient lattice by D=⟨𝒳⟩D=\langle\mathcal{X}\rangle, of height t≤nt\leq n. If 𝒳\mathcal{X} contains neither endpoint of DD, Birkhoff’s theorem (Theorem 4.1) identifies its members with nonempty proper ideals of a poset of size tt. They remain irredundant as subsets of that poset, since meets and joins are intersections and unions. Lemmas 5.4 and 5.6 give |𝒳|≤f⁡(t)≤f⁡(n)|\mathcal{X}|\leq f(t)\leq f(n).

If 𝒳\mathcal{X} contains the greatest element TT of DD and has another member, then ⋁(𝒳∖{T})<T\bigvee(\mathcal{X}\setminus\{T\})<T by irredundance. The lattice generated by the remaining members has height at most t−1t-1, since each of its chains extends by TT. Thus |𝒳|≤1+g⁡(n−1)|\mathcal{X}|\leq 1+g(n-1). The singleton case is immediate, and the least-element case is dual. Consequently

g⁡(n)≤max⁡{f⁡(n),1+g⁡(n−1)}(n≥3).g(n)\leq\max\{f(n),1+g(n-1)\}\qquad(n\geq 3).

For n=3n=3 this gives g⁡(3)≤4=f⁡(3)g(3)\leq 4=f(3). Since f⁡(n)≥f⁡(n−1)+1f(n)\geq f(n-1)+1 for n≥4n\geq 4, induction completes the proof. ∎

Remark 5.8.

The bound is sharp for every n≥3n\geq 3. Choose a tree on an nn-element set Ω\Omega. For each oriented edge α→β\alpha\to\beta, take the component containing α\alpha after deleting that edge. Among the 2​n−22n-2 resulting sets, only this one violates α∈S⇒β∈S\alpha\in S\Rightarrow\beta\in S, so they are irredundant by (5.2). Example 5.5 is the three-vertex case.

For n≥4n\geq 4, partition Ω=Ξ⊔Υ\Omega=\Xi\sqcup\Upsilon as equally as possible, with Ξ={ξ1,…,ξp}\Xi=\{\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{p}\} and Υ={η1,…,ηq}\Upsilon=\{\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{q}\}. The p​qpq sets

Si​j={ξi}∪(Υ∖{ηj})S_{ij}=\{\xi_{i}\}\cup(\Upsilon\setminus\{\eta_{j}\})

are irredundant, since only Si​jS_{ij} violates ξi∈S⇒ηj∈S\xi_{i}\in S\Rightarrow\eta_{j}\in S. As p​q=⌊n2/4⌋pq=\lfloor n^{2}/4\rfloor, we obtain g⁡(n)=f⁡(n)g(n)=f(n) for all n≥3n\geq 3.

5.3 The upper bound

Proposition 5.9.

For every r≥2r\geq 2,

hdist​(r)≤max⁡{r+1, 2​r−3,⌊(r−1)24⌋+1}.h_{\mathrm{dist}}(r)\leq\max\left\{r+1,\,2r-3,\,\left\lfloor\frac{(r-1)^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor+1\right\}.
Proof.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a minimal failure with mm members in a rank rr matroid. By Lemma 5.2(c), it suffices to bound mm; assume m>r+1m>r+1. Some one-member deletion ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} has no common adapted basis. Otherwise every subfamily of at most r+1r+1 members would have one, and Theorem 3.1 would give a common adapted basis for ℱ\mathcal{F}, contradicting its nondistributivity.

The lattice D′=⟨ℱ′⟩D^{\prime}=\langle\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\rangle is finite and distributive, and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is irredundant. Its height is at most r−1r-1: height rr would give a common adapted basis by Corollary 4.6. Hence m−1≤g⁡(r−1)m-1\leq g(r-1). For r=2,3r=2,3, Proposition 5.7 gives m≤r+1m\leq r+1, a contradiction. For r≥4r\geq 4 it gives

m≤1+f⁡(r−1)=max⁡{2​r−3,⌊(r−1)24⌋+1},m\leq 1+f(r-1)=\max\left\{2r-3,\,\left\lfloor\frac{(r-1)^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor+1\right\},

as required. ∎

5.4 The graphic lower bound

Let p,q≥2p,q\geq 2. The graph Gp,qG_{p,q} consists of q+1q+1 internally disjoint paths from uu to vv. The qq short paths are u,xj,vu,x_{j},v, with edges bj=u​xjb_{j}=ux_{j} and cj=xj​vc_{j}=x_{j}v. The long path is u,y1,…,yp,vu,y_{1},\ldots,y_{p},v, with edges a1=u​y1a_{1}=uy_{1}, ai=yi−1​yia_{i}=y_{i-1}y_{i} for 2≤i≤p2\leq i\leq p, and w=yp​vw=y_{p}v. Its cycle matroid Mp,qM_{p,q} has rank p+q+1p+q+1. Figure 1 shows G3,3G_{3,3}.

Over any field, Mp,qM_{p,q} is represented by

ai,bj,cj=bj+z,w=a1+⋯+ap+z,a_{i},\qquad b_{j},\qquad c_{j}=b_{j}+z,\qquad w=a_{1}+\cdots+a_{p}+z, (5.3)

where a1,…,ap,b1,…,bq,za_{1},\ldots,a_{p},b_{1},\ldots,b_{q},z are independent auxiliary vectors and zz is not a ground element. Indeed, assign potentials 0,z,−bj0,z,-b_{j} and −(a1+⋯+ai)-(a_{1}+\cdots+a_{i}) to u,v,xju,v,x_{j} and yiy_{i}, respectively. Orient bj,aib_{j},a_{i} towards uu along their paths and cj,wc_{j},w towards vv. The edge differences are the displayed vectors, and the nonzero vertex potentials form a basis, giving a change of coordinates in the reduced incidence representation.

Set Ω=Ξ⊔Υ\Omega=\Xi\sqcup\Upsilon, where Ξ={ξ1,…,ξp}\Xi=\{\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{p}\} and Υ={η1,…,ηq}\Upsilon=\{\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{q}\}. For S⊆ΩS\subseteq\Omega, put

RS={ai:ξi∈S}∪⋃ηj∈S{bj,cj},FS=cl⁡(RS).R_{S}=\{a_{i}:\xi_{i}\in S\}\cup\bigcup_{\eta_{j}\in S}\{b_{j},c_{j}\},\qquad F_{S}=\cl(R_{S}).
Lemma 5.10.

For every S⊆ΩS\subseteq\Omega,

FS={RS∪{w},Ξ⊆S​ and ​S∩Υ≠∅,RS,otherwise,rk⁡(FS)=|S|+𝟏S∩Υ≠∅.F_{S}=\begin{cases}R_{S}\cup\{w\},&\Xi\subseteq S\text{ and }S\cap\Upsilon\neq\varnothing,\\ R_{S},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\rk(F_{S})=|S|+\mathbf{1}_{S\cap\Upsilon\neq\varnothing}. (5.4)

The map S↦FSS\mapsto F_{S} is injective and satisfies FS∨FT=FS∪TF_{S}\vee F_{T}=F_{S\cup T}.

Proof.

By (5.3), RSR_{S} spans the independent auxiliary vectors aia_{i} with ξi∈S\xi_{i}\in S, bjb_{j} with ηj∈S\eta_{j}\in S, and also zz when S∩Υ≠∅S\cap\Upsilon\neq\varnothing. This gives the rank formula. A ground element belongs to this span exactly when all auxiliary vectors in its expression occur among these vectors, giving the closure formula. Finally, FS∖{w}=RSF_{S}\setminus\{w\}=R_{S} determines SS, and

FS∨FT=cl⁡(RS∪RT)=FS∪T.F_{S}\vee F_{T}=\cl(R_{S}\cup R_{T})=F_{S\cup T}.

∎

Proposition 5.11.

The p​qpq distinct flats

Hi​j=F{ξi}∪(Υ∖{ηj})={ai}∪⋃k≠j{bk,ck}(1≤i≤p, 1≤j≤q)H_{ij}=F_{\{\xi_{i}\}\cup(\Upsilon\setminus\{\eta_{j}\})}=\{a_{i}\}\cup\bigcup_{k\neq j}\{b_{k},c_{k}\}\qquad(1\leq i\leq p,\ 1\leq j\leq q)

form a minimal failure of distributive generation in Mp,qM_{p,q}.

Proof.

The displayed description and distinctness follow from Lemma 5.10, since p≥2p\geq 2.

First omit one member Hi​jH_{ij}. The labels of all remaining members satisfy ξi∈S⇒ηj∈S\xi_{i}\in S\Rightarrow\eta_{j}\in S and hence belong to the distributive lattice Li​jL_{ij} of subsets satisfying this implication. The map S↦FSS\mapsto F_{S} preserves joins by Lemma 5.10. It also preserves meets on Li​jL_{ij}: we have RS∩RT=RS∩TR_{S}\cap R_{T}=R_{S\cap T}, and if w∈FS∩FTw\in F_{S}\cap F_{T}, both labels contain Ξ\Xi, so the implication puts ηj\eta_{j} in both. Thus w∈FS∩Tw\in F_{S\cap T}. Together with injectivity, this shows that the image of Li​jL_{ij} is a distributive sublattice containing all remaining Hk​lH_{kl}. Every proper subfamily is therefore distributive.

The full family generates

Xi=⋂j=1qHi​j={ai},Yj=⋂i=1p⋂k≠jHi​k={bj,cj}.X_{i}=\bigcap_{j=1}^{q}H_{ij}=\{a_{i}\},\qquad Y_{j}=\bigcap_{i=1}^{p}\ \bigcap_{k\neq j}H_{ik}=\{b_{j},c_{j}\}.

Here q≥2q\geq 2 ensures the second intersection has a nonempty index set, and p≥2p\geq 2 removes all aia_{i}. Put FΞ=⋁iXi={a1,…,ap}F_{\Xi}=\bigvee_{i}X_{i}=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{p}\}. For distinct j,kj,k, Lemma 5.10 gives

FΞ∨(Yj∧Yk)=FΞ⊊(FΞ∨Yj)∧(FΞ∨Yk)=FΞ∪{w}.F_{\Xi}\vee(Y_{j}\wedge Y_{k})=F_{\Xi}\ \subsetneq\ (F_{\Xi}\vee Y_{j})\wedge(F_{\Xi}\vee Y_{k})=F_{\Xi}\cup\{w\}.

Thus the dual distributive law fails. ∎

Completion of the proof of Theorem 5.1.

Example 5.3 gives the lower bound r+1r+1. For r≥5r\geq 5, choose p=⌊(r−1)/2⌋p=\lfloor(r-1)/2\rfloor and q=⌈(r−1)/2⌉q=\lceil(r-1)/2\rceil. Then p,q≥2p,q\geq 2, and Proposition 5.11 gives a minimal failure of size p​q=⌊(r−1)2/4⌋pq=\lfloor(r-1)^{2}/4\rfloor in rank rr. This bound exceeds r+1r+1 exactly when r≥7r\geq 7. The upper bounds are the values of the maximum in Proposition 5.9.

Restricting to a class of matroids preserves the upper bounds. Both lower-bound constructions are graphic, and graphic matroids are representable over every field [13, Chapter 5], so the restricted Helly numbers satisfy the same bounds. ∎
